prompt.context: Our client is a major high-end automotive brand (think BMW, Audi, etc.) looking to expand its racing footprint into the Formula 1 (F1) space. Our client understands that this is an area that would require significant capital to produce a competitive team capable of winning at least 3 races each year. Further, our client is interested in the different options of joining, either by sponsoring an existing team or creating a new team as a manufacturer (called a constructor).
prompt.question: We are now tasked with helping our client to determine the viability of entering the F1 market. Should the client enter F1, and if so, as a constructor or as a sponsor?

clarifying_info.a: Formula 1 is a global racing league with 10 teams each consisting of 2 drivers. Teams can either be constructors (make their own cars and engines) or sponsors (purchase manufactured parts from a constructor and generate revenue through selling sponsor space on the car).

clarifying_info.q: How many races are in a season?

clarifying_info.a: Our client is looking for a net positive NPV project. They also base all new projects off a 10% discount rate.

clarifying_info.q: How do F1 teams make money?
clarifying_info.a: Evenly split distributions from F1, race winnings, and advertising.

exhibits.title: Cost Analysis
exhibits.shows: A table comparing annual costs for a Constructor vs. a Sponsor across factory CAPEX, R&D, production per car, fuel per gallon, tires per set, maintenance per race, and driver contracts. Sponsor costs are expressed as a percentage of constructor costs.

data.Note: Sponsor costs are expressed as a % of constructor costs and are in addition to constructor costs

framework: Constructor NPV: revenues (F1 payout, race winnings, advertising) minus costs (factory CAPEX, R&D, production, fuel/tires/maintenance, driver contracts) discounted at 10%
Sponsor NPV: revenues (sponsorship deal winnings, advertising) minus costs (driven by sponsorship deal percentages of constructor costs) discounted at 10%
Internal considerations: cash on hand, funding sources, risk profile, alignment with customer base, technological feasibility to build a competitive car
External considerations: future of F1 (shift to electric?), changing fuel costs, access to suitable drivers from the driver pool

questions.prompt: What are the potential sources of revenue for the client under each entry option?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify F1 distributed funds, race winnings, and advertising as the three revenue streams. Strong candidates will proactively note that the FIA governing body distributes funds to teams. After the candidate identifies these three streams, provide: total F1 revenues = $1B; half ($500M) split evenly across 10 teams (constructors only receive this; sponsors receive none); other half ($500M) split evenly as race winnings (all to first place), team wins 3 races (sponsor deal covers only the first 3 wins, constructor retains all); advertising = $130M for constructors, 20% of that ($26M) for sponsors.

math.setup: Calculate annual revenue for Constructor and Sponsor separately. F1 payout: $1B x 50% / 10 teams. Race winnings: $1B x 50% / 20 races x 3 wins. Advertising: given directly.
steps: Race winnings (Sponsor): same 3 wins but capped at first 3 = $75M

questions.prompt: Analyze Exhibit 1 and calculate total annual operating costs for both the Constructor and Sponsor options. Then compute NPV for each.
questions.guidance: Candidate must work through each line item using the additional assumptions: F1 cars get 0.75 mpg, ~300 miles per race weekend, 20 race weekends, 2 cars per team; 10 sets of tires per race weekend, 20 weekends, 2 cars; maintenance 2 cars x 20 weekends; 2 drivers at same contract value. Under the sponsorship deal the client incurs no up-front CAPEX and no fuel costs (covered by another sponsor). Remaining sponsor percentages apply to total constructor costs. After completing cost analysis, round operating costs to $200M (constructor) and $100M (sponsor). CAPEX is year 0 (no discounting). Discount rate 10%, perpetuity.

math.setup: Calculate each OpEx line for Constructor, apply percentages for Sponsor, sum to OpEx, then NPV = (Annual Profit / discount rate) - CAPEX.
steps: Fuel (Constructor): $15/gal x (300mi / 0.75mpg) x 20 weekends x 2 cars = $15 x 400 x 20 x 2 = $240,000 ≈ $0.24M; Sponsor: $0 (covered)
Tires (Constructor): $4,000/set x 10 sets x 20 weekends x 2 cars = $1.6M; Sponsor: 25% x $1.6M = $0.4M
math.answer: Constructor NPV = $75M (positive, above hurdle rate); Sponsor NPV = $10M (positive but much smaller)

brainstorming.prompt: What qualitative factors should our client consider surrounding this decision?

categories.name: Current Competitive Landscape
ideas: Are 3 race wins per season actually achievable given current team performance?
Are suitable drivers available to sign?
Does the client have sufficient cash on hand for the required CAPEX?

categories.name: Future of F1
ideas: Potential shift to electric vehicles misaligning with current powertrain investment
Changes in fuel prices affecting operational cost assumptions
Changes in annual production budget rules
Changes in revenue split by the FIA

categories.name: Alternatives
ideas: Entering other racing leagues (e.g., Formula E, IndyCar, Le Mans) instead
Partnering with movies or entertainment properties for brand exposure
Sponsoring the F1 league itself rather than a specific team

recommendation: Our client should enter F1 as a constructor. The constructor option yields a positive NPV of $75M, which exceeds the client's required 10% return, compared to only $10M for the sponsor route. As a constructor the client captures full F1 distribution payouts and retains all race winnings, producing significantly higher annual profits of ~$60M vs. ~$1M.
risks: The future of F1 may shift toward electric vehicles, potentially misaligning with the client's current brand and technology
Early competitiveness is uncertain — achieving 3 wins per season in the initial years may be difficult, compressing actual returns below the model
The $525M CAPEX requirement must be fully funded up front at Year 0
next_steps: Conduct a competitive landscape analysis of existing F1 teams and the driver pool to assess the realistic feasibility of building a team capable of winning 3 races per season quickly
Evaluate the client's balance sheet and financing options to confirm the $525M CAPEX can be executed without constraining core business operations
